passage: On a wet Sunday, ten-year-old Pranav opened a building set with four hundred pieces and a picture of a crane on the box. His mother Rekha called him for lunch. He did not hear. She called again, and he waved a hand. When she came in, the plate was cold, the light had changed, and he was fitting the last arm in place, tongue between his teeth. "Was it hard?" she asked. "Just hard enough," he said, and blinked as if waking up. Five years later, Pranav sat cross-legged with a guitar, working a chord change that kept buzzing. His friend Kunal texted about a game night, and the phone buzzed on the bed. Pranav did not touch it. He played the change slowly, then a bit faster, until his fingers landed clean. When he looked up, an hour had gone. His shoulders were loose and his mind felt clear. He picked up the phone at last, typed to Kunal that he'd come after dinner, and went back to the strings for one more round.

qa.q: What was pictured on the box of Pranav's building set?
qa.a: The box had a picture of a crane on it.

qa.q: How is Pranav's absorption at ten similar to and different from his practice at fifteen?
qa.a: At ten he lost track of lunch and light while building the crane, and at fifteen he lost track of time and his phone while working the chord change. Both tasks were hard enough to need his attention, and both left him calm and clear.

qa.q: What was Pranav probably feeling when he said the crane was just hard enough?
qa.a: He felt quietly satisfied and pleasantly challenged, and he seemed to wake up from being absorbed.

qa.q: What could Pranav do to keep enjoying this kind of focus?
qa.a: He could pick pieces or songs a little harder than the last, and keep his phone away while he works on them. 🙂

grounding: The same person shows flow at two ages: absorbed in a building set as a child and in guitar practice as a teenager, when the task suits his skill.

passage: At nine, Jyoti's painting was crumpled by a classmate at recess, and the whole afternoon turned grey. At bedtime she told her father Shankar that the whole week had been bad, the spelling test, the rainy walk, the lost pencil, and that tomorrow would be terrible too. She could not remember the good bits at all. At fifteen, Jyoti's low mood had lasted for weeks. A friend's message saying "ok see you" looked to her like a cold brush-off, and she scrolled through her memory finding only failures. She stopped eating lunch with the others. One evening Shankar noticed she had not smiled all week, and he sat on the bed and said, "I'm worried about you. Would you talk with the school counsellor with me tomorrow?" She nodded, and that morning he phoned to ask for a time. At twenty, Jyoti got an unexpected high grade and floated through the day. When Pankaj asked her to take on his shifts, help with a fest and join a trip that same weekend, she said yes three times, laughing. Only later, looking at her calendar, did she wonder what she had agreed to.

qa.q: What did Jyoti tell her father at bedtime when she was nine?
qa.a: She told him that the whole week had been bad and tomorrow would be terrible too.

qa.q: How does Jyoti's mood shape what she recalls and expects at nine, fifteen and twenty?
qa.a: At nine and fifteen her low mood made her recall only bad things and read a friendly message as a brush-off, while at twenty a great mood made her say yes to three requests without weighing risks. In each case her mood chose which thoughts came to mind.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when she read "ok see you" as a cold brush-off?
qa.a: She felt hurt and rejected, because her weeks of low mood made a neutral message look unkind.

qa.q: How could Shankar support Jyoti after her low mood lasted for weeks?
qa.a: He can stay close, listen without arguing, and take her to the school counsellor, as he did, so a caring professional can help.

grounding: The same person's mood tilts her thinking at three ages: a sad child recalling only bad things, a low-mood teenager reading rejection, and a happy young adult underestimating risks.

passage: Two-year-old Hafsa toddled behind her grandfather on the veranda and picked up the spoon he had dropped, holding it up with both hands. Nobody had asked her to, and she wanted no biscuit for it. She simply placed it on the table and walked off. At fifteen, Hafsa noticed that her classmate Devika, who wore a hearing aid, was left out of the group project again. Hafsa moved her chair beside Devika's and said to the group, "Let's plan it so everybody can hear." That Saturday she joined the school's clean-water drive and gave up her cricket practice to hand out leaflets. At twenty-five, Hafsa turned down a higher-paying job so that she could work at a small organisation that maps clean water sources in villages. She rented a smaller flat, put aside part of her salary for a scholarship fund, and arranged her weekends around volunteering. Her colleague Payal asked if she ever regretted it. Hafsa looked at the map on the wall, covered in pins. "Not once," she said.

qa.q: What did Hafsa pick up on the veranda when she was two?
qa.a: She picked up the spoon her grandfather had dropped.

qa.q: How does Hafsa's helping at two connect to her choices at fifteen and twenty-five?
qa.a: At two she helped without being asked or rewarded, at fifteen she stood up for Devika and joined the water drive, and at twenty-five she built her job, home and weekends around that same care for others. Her care grew from picking up a dropped spoon into a mission.

qa.q: What was Devika probably feeling before Hafsa moved her chair beside hers?
qa.a: She felt left out and lonely, since the group had once again planned without her.

qa.q: What could Payal do to support Hafsa's mission?
qa.a: Payal could volunteer for a weekend on the water mapping, share the map with others, or help raise money for the scholarship fund.

grounding: One person's prosocial care grows across three ages: picking up dropped items unprompted as a toddler, standing up for a peer and volunteering at fifteen, and organising her career around service at twenty-five.

passage: Five-year-old Charu was colouring when her uncle's harsh, booming voice came from the next room. She froze, crayon in the air, sure he was angry with her. Her aunt knelt down and said, "He's shouting at the cricket on the phone, not at you." Charu's shoulders came down. At twenty, Charu was in the audience when her classmate Sachin began his final presentation in a shaking voice. She wondered if he was scared, upset or just excited. She did not decide. She smiled, kept her eyes friendly, and waited. Afterwards she said, "Your voice was wobbling at the start. Was it nerves, or something else?" Sachin exhaled. "Nerves. My grandmother is in the hall." At twenty-five, Charu worked in customer service when a client named Imran phoned, his voice rough and strained. "This is the third time I have complained," he rasped. Charu sat up, lowered her own voice and slowed down. "I can hear how frustrating this has been. Let me note exactly what went wrong." After a moment, his voice eased.

qa.q: What was Charu doing when she heard her uncle's voice?
qa.a: She was colouring when she heard her uncle's harsh, booming voice.

qa.q: How do the voices Charu hears at five, twenty and twenty-five differ, and how does she treat each?
qa.a: At five a harsh, booming voice frightened her because she thought her uncle was angry with her; at twenty she waited, smiled and asked about Sachin's trembling voice; at twenty-five she lowered her own voice and slowed down for Imran's strained, rough voice. The voice showed strong feeling without saying why.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when her uncle's voice boomed from the next room?
qa.a: She felt frightened and thought her uncle was angry with her, as her frozen crayon shows.

qa.q: What could Charu do next time a caller's voice is strained and rough?
qa.a: She could keep her voice low and slow, name the frustration she hears, and then make a clear plan for what she will do next.

grounding: The same person reads voice quality at three ages: a child fearing a harsh voice, a peer's trembling voice met with warmth and a question, and an angry client calmed by a lowered voice.

passage: Age nine. Payal held the ladder at the foot of the mango tree while her little brother climbed to the highest branch. "I won't fall," he called. "Falling is for other people." The branch cracked; he grabbed the trunk, scraped his elbow, and came down slower than he went up. Age fifteen. Sangeeta zipped up her jacket and climbed onto the back of a friend's scooter without a helmet. "I'm always careful. Accidents happen to careless people." Her mother, waiting at the gate, held out a spare helmet and said, "Wear it or walk with me." Sangeeta rolled her eyes, put it on, and rode away. Age twenty-one. Kavitha graduated in June and had her plans set: a great first job by July, a flat by August, savings piling up, and the friend she'd been seeing to become permanent. She had no other applications out. In September the job offer was withdrawn. Kavitha sat with her laptop open on an empty inbox, and only then asked her older cousin how she had managed her first year.

qa.q: What did the little brother call from the mango tree?
qa.a: He called, "I won't fall. Falling is for other people."

qa.q: What do the boy in the tree, Sangeeta on the scooter and Kavitha after graduation share?
qa.a: Each expected the bad outcome to happen to other people: the brother expected not to fall, Sangeeta believed accidents happen to careless people, and Kavitha planned on the first job, the flat and the relationship without another plan. In the end the branch cracked and the offer was withdrawn.

qa.q: What was Kavitha probably feeling as she sat with the empty inbox?
qa.a: She felt shocked and anxious, since she had built everything on one hope and had no other plan.

qa.q: What could Kavitha do next to make her hopes more solid?
qa.a: She could start other applications, keep some savings in reserve and talk to her cousin about what worked in the first year.

grounding: Three separate vignettes marked by age show optimism bias growing up: a boy sure he cannot fall, a teenager sure a scooter ride is safe, and a graduate who plans without a backup.

passage: Two-year-old Harsha sat in the corner of the sofa with his thumb in his mouth and a fold of his mother's dupatta pressed to his cheek. It was late afternoon, he was tired, and a stranger had visited earlier. His mother Shalini did not pull the thumb away. She sat beside him and let him settle. At fifteen, he waited outside the class to give a presentation, rubbing the back of his neck and touching his face. He bit a nail. Then he slowed his breath the way his teacher had shown him, and walked in more steadily. At twenty, Harsha attended a long lecture and clicked his pen without stopping, one foot bouncing under the desk. It helped him hold on to the words. The student beside him, Gurpreet, glanced at the clicking, then at his notes. "The clicking is helping you concentrate, isn't it?" Harsha looked startled. "Yeah. Does it bother you?" Gurpreet shook his head. "I'd rather ask than assume." Harsha nodded and went on writing.

qa.q: Where was Harsha sitting with his thumb in his mouth?
qa.a: He sat in the corner of the sofa.

qa.q: How does Harsha settle himself at two, fifteen and twenty, and what do they have in common?
qa.a: At two he sucked his thumb and held a fold of the dupatta, at fifteen he rubbed his neck and bit a nail before slowing his breath, and at twenty he clicked a pen and bounced a foot to focus. Each movement helped calm or focus him and was not a sign of rudeness.

qa.q: What was Harsha probably feeling while waiting outside the class to present?
qa.a: He felt nervous, as his rubbing of the neck and biting of a nail show, but he steadied himself with slow breathing.

qa.q: What could Gurpreet do if Harsha's pen clicking began to disturb other students?
qa.a: Gurpreet could ask Harsha kindly whether there is a quieter way to do it, such as a silent fidget, rather than telling him to stop.

grounding: The same person regulates himself with movement at three ages: thumb-sucking as a toddler, self-touch before a presentation, and pen-clicking and foot-bouncing as a young adult.
